forbidden_claims: "The hospital turned her away." It did not. It never called her.
"The hospital refused to treat her because of her insurance."

"The hospital's delay killed her" / "she would have lived if they had seen her." THE SINGLE MOST LIKELY FACTUAL FAILURE IN THIS EPISODE. Death was attributed to hypovolemic shock at a different facility; the damages affirmed were for her suffering while waiting and the family's grief.
Any dramatised account of her final minutes beyond what the opinion records.
"The hospital had done this to other patients" / "this was routine."
Any characterisation of the receptionist or any individual member of staff.
"The court found the hospital dumped her" / "the court ruled the transfer was illegal." The First Circuit expressly declined to review the improper-transfer finding (footnote 7).
"EMTALA guarantees you treatment at any emergency room."
"The court decided families can sue under EMTALA for their own grief." That argument was held waived, never decided.
"Every hospital in America is covered by EMTALA."

THE LINE THE EPISODE IS BUILT ON, verbatim from the opinion: EMTALA should be read to proscribe both actual and CONSTRUCTIVE dumping of patients. The hospital never said no. It simply never called her number. That distinction is the whole film and it is the court's own reasoning, not ours.
